pages.title: Welcome
pages.content:
Welcome to the course on learning PHP.

What will you learn here?

- All the basic concepts of the PHP programming language like - Variables, Strings, Conditions, Arrays, Loops, Functions, etc.
- By the end of this course, you will be able to write code in PHP to solve logical real-world problems.
Let the fun begin!

**Click on Next on the right-hand side to start.**

practiceProblems.title: Comments
practiceProblems.description:
Observe the code in the code editor. It has some grey lines. These are called comments. Comments are lines that don't affect the code in any way. These are just for our reference and to better understand our code. We will be using comments like these to explain the code or to give you instructions on what to do. 

You can make your own comments by starting any line with double slashes **//** or **#**

This will make the whole line a comment and whatever is in that line will not be considered part of the code when executing the code. 

You can also make multi-line comments by starting the body of your comments by /* and ending it with */. 

Look at the comments inside the code editor for better reference.

practiceProblems.title: Printing text
practiceProblems.description:
In the last lesson, we saw how to print a number (using  **`echo`**).

To print a number we write this:
```php
echo 10;
```

But to output a text, we do this:
```php
echo "I love PHP";
```

This will print **I love PHP** to the screen. Notice how **I love PHP** is written inside "" (double quotes). You always have to enclose your text in double quotes ("") when printing.

### Task
In this problem, we want you to output **"I love PHP"**. For that, you have to edit the code present in editor. The editor has some __ (underscores). Your task is to remove underscores and write "I love PHP", to solve the problem.

We add underscores in editor so that you know which portion of code to edit.

Click on Submit after you have edited the code in editor.

practiceProblems.title: Area & Perimeter of Rectangle
practiceProblems.description:
Write a program for the following problem:
- Let’s consider a rectangle of sides 11 and 13.
- Find and output area of the rectangle having length as 11 and breadth as 13
- Find and output perimeter of the rectangle having length as 11 and breadth as 13

For any rectangle, the formula for area is length * breadth. \
The formula for perimeter is 2 * (length + breadth)

**Expected output**
```cpp
143
48
```

practiceProblems.title: Multiple outputs using a single line
practiceProblems.description:
You can also have multiple outputs together in a single  `"echo"`  command. \
They are joined together using the  **`"."`**  symbol.

So, for example,
```php
echo 2;
echo PHP_EOL;
echo 3;
```
and
```php
echo 2 . PHP_EOL . 3;
```
are equivalent.

### Task
Write a program to output 7 and 3 on two lines, using a single echo statement.

practiceProblems.title: Inserting space between outputs
practiceProblems.description:
If you want the output to be in the same line and have a space separate them,
- We can use " " to act as an empty space in between multiple outputs. 
- We had seen previously that text has to be enclosed within double quotes during  `echo`  ("text")
- An empty space is a blank space between double quotes (" ")

For example, to print: **2 2**, we can write
```php
echo 2 . " " . 2;
```

### Task
Write a program to output 7 and 3 on a single line, space separated, using a single cout statement.


practiceProblems.title: Variables
practiceProblems.description:
A **variable** is like a labeled box where you can store data. Imagine you have a box labeled "age" and you put the number 25 in it. In PHP, you would do this by writing `$age = 25;`. This means you're storing the number 25 in the variable named `age`. In PHP, the dollar sign $ is used to denote the start of a variable. By using the dollar sign, PHP can distinguish between variables and other elements like functions, keywords, and constants.

Here's the cool part: whenever you use `age` in your code, PHP will remember it is 25. For example, if you write **`echo age`**, PHP will show 25.

### Task
- Create a variable in editor named `age` and assign the value 25 to it.
- Print the value of `age` variable using print statement.

practiceProblems.title: Properties of Variables
practiceProblems.description:
We learned that variable is a labelled box which can store many different types of values. You can also change the value of a variable in your code.

For example
```php
// Declare a variable
$age = 25;
echo $age.PHP_EOL;

// Update age
$age = 26;
echo $age;
```

The above code will output
```php
25
26
```

We are going to use variables all the time in the coming lessons. So let's learn a few more stuff about them.

**Rules for PHP variable names:**
- Must start with a Dollar sign ($).
- A variable name can contain letters, numbers, and underscores (i.e., `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, and `_`).
- After the initial **`$`** and letter or underscore, you can use any combination of letters, numbers, and underscores.  
  (For example: **`$variable_name`**, **`$var123`**, **`$var_name2`**).
- A variable name cannot have spaces in between.
- Variable names are case-sensitive (**`age`**, **`Age`** and **`AGE`**  are three different variables).
- Variable names cannot be any of the reserved keywords in PHP (e.g., **`function`**, **`echo`**, **`while`**, **`class`**, **`return`**, etc.). These keywords have special meanings in the language and are used to define the syntax and structure of PHP programs.

Make sure to follow these rules when creating a variable to not get errors.

### Task
There is some code written in the editor to print the number 8. But the variable name is not following the rule. Can you spot the mistake and fix it?

practiceProblems.title: Variable Datatype
practiceProblems.description:
In PHP, you don't need to explicitly specify the type of a variable during declaration. The type is inferred based on the kind of value assigned to the variable.

For example if you put decimal values in a variable, the type of variable becomes float.

```cpp
$pi = 3.14;
```


### Task
Write a program which does the following:
- Find the area of a circle whose radius is **8.9**. Take `pi = 3.14`
- Declare  `variables`  **`radius`**,  **`pi`**  and  **`area`**  and assign the relevant values to them
- Formula for area of a circle is Pi * radius * radius

practiceProblems.title: Boolean Datatype
practiceProblems.description:
In programming, you often need to know if something is true or false.\
For this, we can have  `variables`  containing just one of these two values -  `true`  or  `false`.

These  `variables`  are called **`"boolean"`** variables.\
We will look at applications of these in later modules.

Example:

```php
$x = true;
```

### Task
Write a program which does the following:

pages.title: Type conversion
pages.content:
### Type Conversion in PHP

In PHP, type conversion works similarly to other programming languages, with both implicit and explicit conversions. Here’s how each type of conversion works:

#### Implicit Type Conversion
PHP automatically converts a variable from one data type to another when necessary.

**Example:**
```php
$x = 7;      // Integer
$x = $x / 2; // Division produces a float
echo $x;     // Output: 3.5
```
Here we declare $x$ as an integer and initialize it to $7$. Then we declare another float variable and set it's value to $x$ which is an integer. Here the integer $7$ which is stored in $x$ is converted to a float and stored in $y$ as $7.0$.


### Explicit Type Conversion
In PHP, you can manually convert a variable from one data type to another using type casting or built-in functions.

**Example using Type Casting:**
```php
$num = '12';      // String
$num = (int)$num; // Convert string to integer
$num = $num + $num; // Arithmetic operation
echo $num;        // Output: 24
```

**Example using Built-in Functions::**
```php
$num = '12';           // String
$num = intval($num);   // Convert string to integer
$num = $num + $num;    // Arithmetic operation
echo $num;             // Output: 24
```

practiceProblems.title: Character Operations
practiceProblems.description:
In PHP, characters are internally represented as their ASCII values, which are integers. This allows us to manipulate characters using arithmetic operations on their ASCII values.

For example:

```php
<?php
// Convert 'a' to its ASCII value, add 1, then convert back to the character
echo chr(ord('a') + 1); // This will output 'b'
```
- The function **`ord('a')`** returns the ASCII value of the character `'a'`, which is `97`.
- By adding `1` to this value (`97 + 1 = 98`), we get the ASCII value of `'b'`, which is `98`.
- The **`chr()`** function then converts the ASCII value `98` back into the character `'b'`.

Similarly, you can reverse this operation. If you subtract `1` from `'b'` and convert it back to a character, you'll get `'a'`:

```php
<?php
// Subtract 1 from the ASCII value of 'b' and convert it back to a character
echo chr(ord('b') - 1); // This will output 'a'
```


### Task 
Convert 'a' to 'e' and output 'e'. Check what value do you have to add to 'a' to get 'e'?

practiceProblems.title: Converting Uppercase Characters to Lowercase
practiceProblems.description:
As we explored earlier, we can manipulate characters using arithmetic operations because their ASCII values are sequentially ordered. This allows us to convert uppercase letters to lowercase by leveraging the difference in their ASCII values.


- **Uppercase letters** (`A-Z`) have ASCII values between 65 (`A`) and 90 (`Z`).
- **Lowercase letters** (`a-z`) have ASCII values between 97 (`a`) and 122 (`z`).

The difference between the ASCII values of an uppercase and its corresponding lowercase letter is **32**. For example, `'A'` (ASCII 65) can be converted to `'a'` (ASCII 97) by adding 32.

#### Example:
```php
$ch = 'A';
echo chr(ord($ch) + 32);  // Outputs 'a'
```

This outputs:

```txt
a
```

You don't need to memorize the number 32; it simply represents the difference between uppercase and lowercase ASCII values. You can easily use this difference to convert any uppercase letter to lowercase.

Observe how the code calculates this difference and converts the letter in the editor.

practiceProblems.title: Assignment Operators
practiceProblems.description:
In programming, assignment operators help you set or change the value of a variable. 

#### Basic Assignment
Here's a simple example:
```php
$length;
$length = 15;
```
In this example, the **`=`** operator sets the value of `length` to 15.

#### Compound Assignment Operators
**Compound Assignment Operators** are just a shorthand way of performing operations on a variable and assigning the result back to the variable.  

**Without** using the compound assignment operators we write -   
```php
$length = 15;
$length = $length + 5;
```
The same thing **using** Compound Assignment Operator would be written as-  
```php
$length = 15;
$length += 5;
```
We can use any other operator in the same way:

- `x -= 5`        *(Subtracts 5 from `x` and assigns the result back to `x`)*
- `x *= 3`        *(Multiplies `x` by 3 and assigns the result back to `x`)*
- `x /= 3`        *(Divides `x` by 3 and assigns the result back to `x`)*
- `x %= 3`        *(Finds the remainder when `x` is divided by 3 and assigns the result back to `x`)*


### Task
- Using an assignment operator, output the remainder when length is divided by 3.

pages.title: Increment and Decrement Operator
pages.content:
In PHP, the **increment** (`++`) and **decrement** (`--`) operators are used to increase or decrease a variable's value by 1.

#### Types of Increment and Decrement Operators:
1. **Pre-Increment or Pre-Decrement**:
   - These operators first modify the value of the variable (increment or decrement by 1) and then return the updated value.
   ```php
   $a = 5;
   echo ++$a . PHP_EOL; // Outputs: 6
   ```
   In this case, `$a` is incremented first, so the output is `6`.

2. **Post-Increment or Post-Decrement**:
   - These operators return the current value of the variable, then modify the variable by increasing or decreasing its value by 1.
   ```php
   $a = 5;
   echo $a++ . PHP_EOL; // Outputs: 5
   echo $a . PHP_EOL;   // Outputs: 6
   ```
   In the first `echo`, the value `5` is returned before incrementing. Then, after the increment, `$a` becomes `6`, which is reflected in the second `echo`.

### Task:
What is the output of the following code?

```php
$x = 4;
echo ++$x . " "; 
echo $x++ . " "; 
echo $x;     
```

practiceProblems.description:
Logical operators allow you to combine multiple conditions to evaluate whether they are **true** or **false**. They are commonly used in decision-making based on multiple criteria.

- **`&&` (Logical AND)**: Returns `1` (true) only if both conditions are true.

  ```php
  ($a > 5 && $a  10 || $a  5)) // returns 1 if (a > 5) is false, and 0 if (a > 5) is true
  ```

### Task:
You are given a variable `$height`. To enter the waterpark, your height must be **strictly greater than 5** and **strictly less than 10**. Apply the condition and output 1 if $height is eligible to enter the waterpark, otherwise output 0.

pages.title: Operator  Precedence and Associativity
pages.content:
You may be familiar with BODMAS (or PEMDAS in some regions) rule for evaluating arithmetic expressions. It says we solve parenthesis first, then divide, then multiply, then add and then subtract. Similarly there are two main rules a program follows to evaluate an arithmetic expression:
- **Precedence** - It tells the priority of operations. 
- **Associativity** - It tells what order the operations with the same priority will be performed in.

pages.title: Operator precedence
pages.content:
Operator precedence means that some operations are done before others when evaluating an expression. Operators with higher precedence are evaluated before those with lower precedence. This concept is similar to the rules of arithmetic, where multiplication and division takes precedence over addition and subtraction.

Here's the order of operator precedence in PHP from highest to lowest:

- Parentheses: `()`
- Postfix operators: `++`, `--`
- Unary operators: `+`, `-`, `!`, `~`, `++`, `--`, `(type)`
- Multiplicative operators: `*`, `/`, `%`
- Additive operators: `+`, `-`
- Relational operators: ``, `=`
- Equality operators: `==`, `!=`
- Logical AND operator: `&&`
- Logical OR operator: `||`
- Assignment operators: `=`, `+=`, `-=` ... and so on

### Task

Given the expression: $a + b * c / d$. Choose the order in which the operations are preformed in the expression.

```php
$name = "Chef";

```

2. Output the value stored in `$fruit` to the console.

practiceProblems.title: Changing Characters in a String
practiceProblems.description:
To change the value of a specific character in a  string:
- We refer to the index number to access the specific character by using the indexing operator **`[]`**
- We then assign the new character (enclosed in single quotes ' ' ) to it.

For example:
```php
$myString = "Chaf";
$myString[2] = 'e';

echo $myString;

// Output:
// Chef
```

Here we changed the character at index 2 of "Chaf" which is 'a' with 'e'. Remember indexing always starts from 0.

practiceProblems.title: Substring
practiceProblems.description:
A substring is a small part of a string.  
For example:  
"World" is a substring of the string "Hello World!"  
In PHP, the `substr()` is a string function which is used to extract a substring from a given string.  

It takes three values:
- the string 
- the starting index of the substring
- the number of characters in the substring
```php
$str = "Hello, World!";
echo substr($str, 7, 5);
```
This outputs 
```php
World
```
It goes to the seventh index which is 'W' and takes 5 characters starting from 'W', which results in 'World'.   
We can even give only the starting index to the substr function.  
In that case it will start from the starting index and go till the end of the string.
```php
$str = "Hello, World!";
echo substr($str, 5);
```
This outputs
```php
, World!
```
as it starts from the fifth index which is ',' and goes till the end of the string. 

Please note that if we provide invalid starting index, the program will throw an error.
### Task
- Update the given code in IDE to print **fruit**.

practiceProblems.title: Taking User Input
practiceProblems.description:
You've already learned how to use `echo` to output values. Now, let's learn how to take input from the user using **`fgets(STDIN)`**.

#### How `fgets(STDIN)` Works:
- **`fgets(STDIN)`** is a predefined function in PHP that reads input from the user through the keyboard.
- To clean the input and remove any unnecessary whitespace, we often use the **`trim()`** function.

#### Example:
```php
$num = trim(fgets(STDIN)); // Reads input and removes any whitespace
```

In the above code, the user input is stored in the variable `$num`.

### Task:
Complete the program in the IDE with the following steps:
1. Declare an integer variable **`$a`**.
2. Take a number as input from the user and assign it to **`$a`**.
3. Output the assigned value of **`$a`** with the text **`"Your number is: "`**.

practiceProblems.title: Taking Multiple User Inputs
practiceProblems.description:
Similar to how we give multiple outputs, we can also take multiple inputs in single line.

```php
$line = trim(fgets(STDIN)); // Read the entire line of input
$inputs = explode(" ", $line); // Split the line into an array of values

$a = intval($inputs[0]); // Convert the first value to an integer
$b = intval($inputs[1]); // Convert the second value to an integer

echo $b . " " . $a . PHP_EOL; // Output the values
```
- **explode(" ", $line)** splits the input string by spaces into an array.
- **intval()** converts the string values to integers.
- An **array** is a collection of items stored at contiguous memory locations, where each item can be accessed by an index or key. 
**We will cover array's in much depth later in this course.** 

In the above code, we read a single line of input, split it into two integers $a$ and $b$ using **explode()**, and then output the values of $b$ and $a$ in that order.

Thus, for the input: 
```php
2 3
```
the output will be: 
```php
3 2
```

### Task
Write a program to take three inputs $a$, $b$ and $c$ and output their sum.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Similar to how we give multiple outputs, we can also take multiple inputs in single line.

```php
$line = trim(fgets(STDIN)); // Read the entire line of input
$inputs = explode(" ", $line); // Split the line into an array of values

$a = intval($inputs[0]); // Convert the first value to an integer
$b = intval($inputs[1]); // Convert the second value to an integer

echo $b . " " . $a . PHP_EOL; // Output the values
```
- **explode(" ", $line)** splits the input string by spaces into an array.
- **intval()** converts the string values to integers.
- An **array** is a collection of items stored at contiguous memory locations, where each item can be accessed by an index or key. 
**We will cover array's in much depth later in this course.** 

In the above code, we read a single line of input, split it into two integers $a$ and $b$ using **explode()**, and then output the values of $b$ and $a$ in that order.

Thus, for the input: 
```php
2 3
```
the output will be: 
```php
3 2
```

Write a program to take three inputs $a$, $b$ and $c$ and output their sum.

pages.title: Need of If-Else
pages.content:
Many times our program needs to take different actions based on some conditions.  

For example, Let's suppose we have to write a program that takes the user's age and tells us if we are old enough to vote or not. In this case our program will behave differently if the age entered by the user is below 18 and if the age is above 18.  

If it is above 18, our program will print "Old enough to vote!". Otherwise, it will print "Not old enough to vote!".   

![](https://cdn.codechef.com/Learning/learn-python-new/vote-age-flowchart.png)   

This different behavior in the program can be achieved through something called "If/Else" Statements in PHP.

This '{' is what is known as curly bracket. \
PHP relies on curly brackets ('{' in the beginning and '}' at the end) to know what part of code is inside the if part of the code and what is not. Whatever is inside curly brackets is considered as one block of code.\
When writing an if or else if you don't mention a block of code using curly brackets it executes only the first statement of the if or else section.

**`Run`**  this code and to identify the  **`compilation error`**. \
Fix the curly braces to solve the problem. The two output statements after if need to be in one block of code using curly brackets.

practiceProblems.title: If & Else Statements
practiceProblems.description:
`if` and `else` can be used together to create conditional statements. These allow you to execute different code based on whether a condition is **true** or **false**.

There are several comparison operators you can use in conditional statements:

- **Equal to**: `==`
- **Not equal to**: `!=`
- **Greater than**: `>`
- **Less than**: `=`
- **Less than or equal to**: `<=`

### Syntax for `if/else` in PHP:
```php
if (condition) {
    // Code to be executed if the condition is true
} else {
    // Code to be executed if the condition is false
}
```

### Task:
Write a program that checks whether a person is old enough to vote.

1. Take two variables: `$age` and `$voting_age`.
2. Set `$voting_age` to `18` and take an integer input to store in `$age`.
3. Compare `$age` with `$voting_age` using an `if/else` statement:
   - Output `"Old enough to vote!"` if the person's age is greater than or equal to `$voting_age`.
   - Output `"Not old enough to vote."` if the person's age is less than `$voting_age`.

practiceProblems.title: Conditions in if statements
practiceProblems.description:
PHP supports the usual logical and mathematical conditions:

- **Equals**: `a == b`
- **Not Equals**: `a != b`
- **Less than**: `a  b`
- **Greater than or equal to**: `a >= b`

### Task

Write a program that performs the following:

1. Take input from the console for two integer variables `$a` and `$b`.
2. Compare the two variables and:
   - Print `"Bravo!"` if `$a` is greater than or equal to `$b`.
   - Print `"Try again"` in all other cases.

pages.title: Debugging
pages.content:
As you progress and learn more advanced concepts in PHP, you'll inevitably make mistakes in your code. Some of these mistakes can be difficult to identify. This is where **debugging** becomes crucial. Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors in your code.

### What is a bug?

A **bug** is an error that causes a program to generate an unexpected output, which is different from the intended or expected output, or sometimes produces no output at all.

### Common Error Types:

- **CE - Compilation Error / Syntax Error**: These occur when the code violates PHP's syntax rules, preventing the program from running.
- **RE - Runtime Error**: These happen when the program crashes or behaves unexpectedly during execution.
- **WA - Wrong Answer / Logical Error**: The program runs without crashing, but the output is incorrect due to a logic flaw in the code.
- **TLE - Time Limit Exceeded**: The program takes too long to execute, usually in competitive programming or time-constrained environments.

We will explore each of these errors in detail and learn how to resolve them in the upcoming lessons.

pages.title: Compilation error (syntax error)
pages.content:
Let’s start with **Syntax Errors**.

When writing code in any programming language, you must follow its syntax rules. If the correct syntax is not followed, PHP will throw a **syntax error**.

#### Example:
In English, a sentence is completed with a full stop (`.`). Similarly, in PHP, we complete each statement with a **semicolon** (`;`).

The following is an example of a syntax error — can you spot why?

```php
$number = 19;
echo $number . PHP_EOL
```

pages.title: Runtime Error
pages.content:
Runtime Error: Generally caused by accessing a negative or unreachable index of a string or an array or dividing a number by 0.

```php
<?php
$arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; // array initialization
echo $arr[0]; // accessing first element of array it prints 1 
echo $arr[-1]; // negative position of array doesn't exist so it will give you runtime error
echo $arr[5]; // this position of array does not exist because position ranges from 0 to (length of array)-1
```

Currently we haven't learnt about arrays - you will encounter some of these cases when we cover our module on arrays.

pages.title: Logical Error or Wrong Answer (WA)
pages.content:
A logical error is an error in a program that occurs when the code compiles and runs without producing any error messages, but it does not produce the expected or desired output.  
Instead, it performs a different computation or provides incorrect results due to a flaw in the algorithm or logic of the program.  
Logical errors are the hardest to find in a program.  

Based on what you have learnt so far - you will encounter logical errors of the following types:
- Incorrect Conditions
- Incorrect Index
- Incorrect variable usage

practiceProblems.title: Mismatched Parenthesis
practiceProblems.description:
In PHP (and most programming languages), **parentheses** must be properly matched. For every opening bracket `(` `{` `[`, there must be a corresponding closing bracket `)` `}` `]` of the same type. If mismatched or missing, it will cause a **syntax error**.

#### Example:
If we try to use different types of opening and closing brackets, PHP will throw a syntax error.

```php
$a = (5 + 7 };  // incorrect due to mismatched parentheses
```

The opening bracket `(` does not match the closing bracket `}`.

#### Corrected Code:
```php
$a = (5 + 7);  // corrected parentheses
```

### Task

You are provided with a program that checks whether a number is **odd** or **even**. The code contains a syntax error. Your task is to **debug** the code and fix the problem.

practiceProblems.title: Incorrect Index
practiceProblems.description:
In PHP, strings use **zero-based indexing**, meaning the first character of a string is at index `0`. Often, forgetting this and using **one-based indexing** can result in a **logical error**, where the program doesn't give the expected output.

#### Example: Program to Print the Last Character of a String

```php
<?php
$n = intval(fgets(STDIN));  // Input length of the string

$s = trim(fgets(STDIN));  // Input string

echo $s[$n] . PHP_EOL;  // Wrong answer, as string uses zero-based indexing

echo $s[$n - 1] . PHP_EOL;  // Right answer (prints last character)
```

#### Explanation:
- The incorrect logic is using `$s[$n]` to access the last character, which is one index beyond the end of the string (since indexing starts at `0`).
- To correctly print the last character, you should use `$s[$n - 1]`, which accounts for zero-based indexing.

### Task

You are tasked with writing a program that:
1. Takes a string as input.
2. Prints the **1st**, **4th**, and **6th** characters of the string.

practiceProblems.title: Creating Arrays
practiceProblems.description:
`Arrays`  are used to store multiple values in a single variable, instead of declaring separate variables for each value.

For example
```php
$cars = ["Ferrari", "Volvo", "Lambo", "Tesla"];
```

You can also store different data types in the same array. PHP arrays can contain strings, numbers, boolean, other arrays etc.

```php
$arr = ["Ferrari", 1, 1.5, true];  // An array with multiple data types
```

- Create an  `Array`  of the first 5 positive integers.
- Once the  `array`  is define - output  `"Done"`  to the console.

practiceProblems.title: Types of Arrays
practiceProblems.description:
In PHP, there are three main types of arrays:


 1. Indexed Arrays (Numeric Index) 

Indexed arrays use numeric indexes to store and access values. Indexing starts from `0`.

Example:
```php
$fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Orange"];
echo $fruits[1];  // Outputs: Banana
```



2. Associative Arrays (Named Keys)

Associative arrays use named keys to store values instead of numeric indexes.

Example:
```php
$age = ["John" => 25, "Jane" => 30];
echo $age["John"];  // Outputs: 25
```



3. Multidimensional Arrays (Arrays Within Arrays) 

Multidimensional arrays contain one or more arrays inside them. These arrays can be accessed using multiple indexes.

Example:
```php
$cars = [
    ["Ferrari", 2020],
    ["Lamborghini", 2019]
];
echo $cars[0][0];  // Outputs: Ferrari
```

practiceProblems.title: Updating Specific Element of the Array
practiceProblems.description:
In PHP, arrays allow you to store multiple values. You can **access** and **update** specific elements in an array using their index or key.

To update an array element, simply assign a new value to the specific index or key.

 For Indexed Arrays:
```php
$fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Orange"];
$fruits[1] = "Mango";  // Updating second element
echo $fruits[1];  // Outputs: Mango
```
- The value at index `1` has been updated from `"Banana"` to `"Mango"`.

For Associative Arrays:
```php
$person = ["name" => "Alice", "age" => 25];
$person["age"] = 30;  // Updating age
echo $person["age"];  // Outputs: 30
```
- The value for the key `"age"` has been updated from `25` to `30`.



Adding New Elements to an Array

You can add new elements to an array by assigning a value to a new index or key.

**For Indexed Arrays:**
```php
$fruits[] = "Pineapple";  // Adds "Pineapple" to the end of the array
```

**For Associative Arrays:**
```php
$person["city"] = "New York";  // Adds a new key-value pair
```

### Task
- Complete the given program by replacing the underscores ( _ ). The goal is to update the second array element to 2, then output the second element to the console.

practiceProblems.title: While Loop
practiceProblems.description:
`Loops`  can execute a block of code as long as a specified condition is reached.\
They are handy because they save time, reduce errors, and they make code more readable.\
The  `while loop`  loops through a block of code as long as a specified condition is true:

Syntax:
```cpp
 while (condition) {
     // code to be executed
 }
```

### Task
Write a program which does the following:
- Declare a  `int` variable  ***`a`***  and initialise it to `0`.
- Use the syntax above to create a  `loop`,  output the following to the console:
  - Print  ***`a`***  in separate lines as long as it is less than 7.
  - Increment  ***`a`***  by 1 in each iteration.

practiceProblems.title: Do While Loop
practiceProblems.description:
The  **`do/while`**  `loop`  is a type of  `while loop`. \
This  `loop`  will execute the code block once, before checking if the condition is true, then it will repeat the 
 `loop`  as long as the condition is true.

**Syntax:**
```cpp
    do {
       // Code to be executed
    }
    while (condition); // The loop continues to iterate as long as the condition is true.
```

### Task
Write a program which does the following:
- Declare an integer  `variable`  ***`i`***  and initialise it to 0.
- Use the  `do/while loop`  to output  ***`i`***  to the console as long as  ***`i`***  is less than 6.

practiceProblems.title: foreach Loop
practiceProblems.description:
The **`foreach`** loop in PHP is used to iterate over arrays. It is simpler and more readable than a `for` loop when you only need to work with arrays.

### Syntax:

```php
foreach ($array as $value) {
    // Code to be executed
}
```

- **`$array`**: The array you want to loop through.
- **`$value`**: Holds the current value of the array for each iteration.

**Example 1: Iterating Through an Indexed Array**

```php
$fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Orange"];
foreach ($fruits as $fruit) {
    echo $fruit . PHP_EOL;
}
```

**Output:**
```
Apple
Banana
Orange
```

**Example 2: Iterating Through an Associative Array**

```php
$person = ["name" => "Alice", "age" => 25];
foreach ($person as $key => $value) {
    echo "$key: $value" . PHP_EOL;
}
```

**Output:**
```
name: Alice
age: 25
```

### Task:

1. Accept an array of strings with 5 city names using user input.
2. Use a `foreach` loop to check if the city "Seattle" is present in the array.
3. If "Seattle" is found, print "YES". If not, print "NO".

pages.title: Predefined Functions
pages.content:
Predefined functions, also known as built-in functions, are functions provided by PHP that you can use directly in your programs without having to define them yourself.

Here are some common categories of predefined functions in PHP:

### 1. **Input/Output Functions**:
- **`echo`**: Outputs data to the console or browser.
- **`print`**: Similar to `echo`, but returns `1` and can be used in expressions.
- **`fgets()`**: Reads a line from an open file or from standard input.

### 2. **Mathematical Functions**:
- **`sqrt()`**: Calculates the square root of a number.
- **`abs()`**: Returns the absolute value of a number.
- **`pow()`**: Raises a number to the power of another (e.g., `pow(2, 3)` returns `8`).
- **`ceil()`**: Rounds a number up to the nearest integer.
- **`floor()`**: Rounds a number down to the nearest integer.

### 3. **Memory Functions**:
- **`memory_get_usage()`**: Returns the memory allocated to the current script.
- **`memory_get_peak_usage()`**: Returns the peak memory usage of the current script.

### 4. **Time Functions**:
- **`time()`**: Returns the current Unix timestamp.
- **`date()`**: Formats a local date and time.
- **`strtotime()`**: Converts an English textual datetime into a Unix timestamp.

### 5. **File Handling Functions**:
- **`fopen()`, `fclose()`**: Opens and closes files.
- **`fread()`, `fwrite()`**: Reads from and writes to files.



For now, let's focus on the **mathematical functions** in PHP, which are useful for performing mathematical calculations in your code. You will learn more about other categories of predefined functions later in the course.

practiceProblems.description:
In PHP, variable scope refers to the accessibility of variables in different parts of the program. There are two main types of scope:



**Global Scope**

- Variables defined **outside** of any function or class are in the **global scope**.
- Global variables can be accessed anywhere in the script, but to use them inside a function, you must declare them as `global`.

**Example:**

```php

```


**Local Scope**

- Variables defined **inside** a function are in the **local scope** and can only be accessed within that function.
- Local variables cannot be accessed outside the function.

**Example:**

```php

```


**Accessing Variables from Different Scopes**

- A function can access both local and global variables.
- If a **local variable** and a **global variable** have the same name, the local variable takes precedence inside the function.

practiceProblems.title: More About Functions
practiceProblems.description:
#### **Passing Arguments by Reference**

In PHP, when you pass arguments to a function **by reference**, the function can modify the original value of the variable. This is done by adding an `&` before the parameter in the function definition.

**Syntax:**

```php
function modifyValue(&$var) {
    $var += 10;
}
```

**Example:**

```php
<?php
function addTen(&$num) {
    $num += 10;
}

$value = 5;
addTen($value);
echo $value;  // Output: 15
```

**Explanation**: In the example, the function `addTen()` modifies the original value of `$value` because it's passed by reference using the `&` symbol.



#### **Variable Number of Arguments**

PHP allows functions to accept a **variable number of arguments** using the `...` (splat) operator. This enables flexibility when you don't know in advance how many arguments will be passed to the function.


```php
function sum(...$numbers) {
    $total = 0;  // Initialize the total to 0
    foreach ($numbers as $number) {  // Iterate over each number
        $total += $number;  // Add each number to the total
    }
    return $total;  // Return the final sum
}
```

**Example:**

```php
<?php
function sum(...$numbers) {
    $total = 0;  // Initialize the total to 0
    foreach ($numbers as $number) {  // Iterate over each number
        $total += $number;  // Add each number to the total
    }
    return $total;  // Return the final sum
}

echo sum(1, 2, 3);  // Output: 6
echo sum(10, 20);   // Output: 30
```

**Explanation**: The `...$numbers` parameter allows the function to accept any number of arguments and treats them as an array.



### Task
Create a PHP function called updateValues that does the following:

- Accepts one argument by reference.
- Accepts a variable number of additional arguments.
- The function should add the sum of the variable number of arguments to the original referenced argument.
- Output the updated value of the referenced argument.

practiceProblems.title: Some useful math functions
practiceProblems.description:
Here are some simple and commonly used math functions in PHP that will help you solve various problems:


1. **`abs(A - B)`**:
   - **Purpose**: Returns the absolute value of the difference between `A` and `B`.
   - **Example**:
     ```php
     echo abs(5 - 10);  // Output: 5
     ```

2. **`A % B`** (% is an operator in PHP, not a function):
   - **Purpose**: Returns the remainder when `A` is divided by `B`.
   - **Example**:
     ```php
     echo 10 % 3;  // Output: 1
     ```

3. **`ceil(X)`**:
   - **Purpose**: Rounds the number `X` upwards to its nearest integer.
   - **Example**:
     ```php
     echo ceil(4.2);  // Output: 5
     ```

4. **`floor(X)`**:
   - **Purpose**: Rounds the number `X` downwards to its nearest integer.
   - **Example**:
     ```php
     echo floor(4.8);  // Output: 4
     ```

5. **`pow(X, Y)`**:
   - **Purpose**: Returns the value of `X` raised to the power of `Y`.
   - **Example**:
     ```php
     echo pow(2, 3);  // Output: 8
     ```

These math functions are straightforward to use and can be very helpful in solving various computational problems. You can now proceed to the IDE and try out these functions with different values.

practiceProblems.description:
In a contest where $N$ **new** users visited the contest, 
- $A$ users just saw the problems and didn’t make any submissions and hence won’t get any rating.
- $B$ users who made a submission but could not solve any problem correctly. Thus, after the contest, they will get a rating in the range $800 - 1000$.
- Everyone else could correctly solve at least $1$ problem. Thus, they will get a rating **strictly greater** than $1000$ after the contest.

You need to output the number of new users in the contest who, after the contest, will get a rating and also the number of new users who will get a rating **strictly greater** than $1000$.

The code given in the IDE uses the concept of **functions**. \
Update the code to solve the problem.

Chef is taking his baby steps into the world of programming.

Given the values of $A$ and $B$, can you help Chef find the [*absolute difference*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_difference) between the correct answer and the value his program prints?

#### Code in the IDE to solve the problem.

You will find the concept of  `test cases`  on various programming platforms such as  `SEED-IT, Codeforces, SEED-IT, Hackerrank`.  What are  **`test cases`**?
- **`Test cases`**  are multiple  **`Inputs`**  - multiple instances of the same problem, all of which have to be solved by your code correctly. 
```cpp

    11 
    13 
    2 
    4 
    9
```

- For each  `test cases`,  prints out the integer  ***`N`***  to console on a separate line (our **[Input mirror](https://www.codechef.com/learn/BP00BC01_V2/problems/GSCV205)** problem).

practiceProblems.title: What are hidden test files and test cases
practiceProblems.description:
So far we dealt with  `test files`  and  `test cases`  which were visible to you.

However, programming platforms typically have **hidden** or **private**  `test files`  and  `test cases`.  What are these?
- **Private**  `test files`  check for the following
  - Test your code for logic
  - Test your code for  `corner cases`  /  `edge cases`
  - Test your code for handling scale -> does your program solve within time and space constraints?
- What do these **private**  `test files`  do?
  - Your code is run on  **`each test case`**  within the private  `test file`
  - This generates your  **`actual output`**
  - This is judged against the  **`expected output`**.\
If the  **`actual output`**  and  **`expected output`**  match, then your code is correct

Click on  **`Next`**  in to proceed.

pages.title: What are custom inputs
pages.content:
You will usually find a  **`custom`**  `inputs`  box in programming problems. \
**`Custom`**  `inputs`  allow you to do the following:
- You are able to see the output generated by your code for inputs defined by you.
- Test your code with your sample inputs.\
This helps you debug  **`Wrong Answers (WA)`**,  **`Runtime Errors (RE)`**  faster.
- Create your own  **`test cases`**. \
In programming problems - you want to find exceptions or  `test cases`  where your code / logic can fail. \
**`Custom`**  `inputs`  allow you to test your code for the same.

Click on  **`Next`**  to proceed.

practiceProblems.title: Difference between Run and Submit
practiceProblems.description:
What is the difference between the  **`Run`**  and  **`Submit`**  buttons?
- **`Run`**  allows you to locally test your code on  **`sample inputs`**  and  **`custom inputs`**.
   - `Custom inputs`  are small inputs - mainly for you to test your code.
- **`Submit`**  sends your code to the online judge to compare your  **`Actual output`**  and the  **`Expected output`**.
   - On submission - your code is checked against multiple `test cases`  which are included in the 
**hidden** or **private** test files.
   - Your code / solution is complete only when you click  **`Submit`**  and get an  **`AC`**  (accepted) verdict.
   - **Note:** Your code can run as expected for your  `custom inputs`  - however, it can fail on the **private** 
 `test files`. \
This means your code is **NOT** solving the problem correctly and needs to be fixed.

options: Maintain modular boundaries, handle edge cases, and ensure optimal algorithmic complexity
Rely on undocumented compiler behaviors and arbitrary memory pointers
Suppress error diagnostics and ignore unexpected input bounds
Execute unbounded linear searches across unsorted large-scale collections
